title: Decline of the Indus Valley (Harappan) cities

verified.text: The Indus Valley, or Harappan, civilisation was at its peak from about 2600 to 1900 BCE, in what is now Pakistan and north-west India.
Its cities, such as Harappa, Mohenjo-daro, Dholavira and Lothal, had planned grid streets, covered drains and bricks of standard sizes.
From around 1900 BCE the big cities were slowly abandoned, and people moved into smaller villages, many further east.
The decline was gradual, over centuries, not a single sudden collapse.
The Indus script has still not been deciphered, so the people's own records cannot be read.
The ruins of Harappa and Mohenjo-daro were excavated in the 1920s.

theories.text: Scientists think weakening monsoon rains and long droughts made farming harder and helped push people out of the cities.
Rivers may have shifted course or dried up, including the Ghaggar-Hakra river system, cutting off water and trade routes.
Trade with Mesopotamia appears to have declined in the same period, which may have weakened the cities.

knownErrors.text: Invading Aryans destroyed the Indus cities
knownErrors.correction: Most scholars now reject the idea that an invasion destroyed the cities; the decline was gradual, likely driven by climate and river changes.
